  filter(
    Driver == "Larson"
  )

  filter(
    Driver == "Logano"
  )

  filter(
    Driver == "Chastain"
  )

    Driver == "Bell"

  )

  )
G7Briscoe <- G7Totals |>
  filter(
    Driver == "Briscoe"
  )
G7Blaney <- G7Totals |>
  filter(
    Driver == "Blaney"
  )
G7Byron <- G7Totals |>
  filter(
    Driver == "Byron"
  )
G7Reddick <- G7Totals |>
  filter(
    Driver == "Reddick"
  )
ggplot()+
  geom_bar(data=G7Totals, aes(x=reorder(Driver, Win), weight= Win), fill="lightgrey") +
  geom_bar(data=G7Larson, aes(x=reorder(Driver, Win), weight= Win), fill="blue") +
  geom_bar(data=G7Logano, aes(x=reorder(Driver, Win), weight= Win), fill="gold") +
  geom_bar(data=G7Chastain, aes(x=reorder(Driver, Win), weight= Win), fill="green") +
  geom_bar(data=G7Bell, aes(x=reorder(Driver, Win), weight= Win), fill="orange") +
  geom_bar(data=G7Hamlin, aes(x=reorder(Driver, Win), weight= Win), fill="purple") +
  geom_bar(data=G7Elliott, aes(x=reorder(Driver, Win), weight= Win), fill="lightblue") +
  geom_bar(data=G7Briscoe, aes(x=reorder(Driver, Win), weight= Win), fill="maroon") +
  geom_bar(data=G7Blaney, aes(x=reorder(Driver, Win), weight= Win), fill="yellow") +
  geom_bar(data=G7Byron, aes(x=reorder(Driver, Win), weight= Win), fill="red") +
  geom_bar(data=G7Reddick, aes(x=reorder(Driver, Win), weight= Win), fill="black") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    x= "Name of Driver",
    y= "Number of Wins in Gen 7 Era",
    title= "If You Ain't First, You're Last",
    subtitle= "Kyle Larson, in the Generation 7 era, has more wins than any other driver.",
    caption= "Source: Racing Reference | By: Beck Frazier"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 20, face = "bold")
  )

Champ10 <- G7Totals |> filter(Driver== "Briscoe" | Driver== "Elliott" | Driver== "Bell" | Driver== "Hamlin" | Driver== "Logano" | Driver== "Larson" | Driver== "Chastain" | Driver== "Blaney" | Driver== "Reddick" | Driver== "Byron")

ggplot() + 
  geom_point(
  data=G7Totals, 
  aes(x=AvSt, y=AvFn, size=Win),
  color="grey",
  alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_point(
    data=Champ10,
    aes(x=AvSt, y=AvFn, size=Win),
    color="red") +
  geom_text_repel(
    data=Champ10,
    aes(x=AvSt, y=AvFn, label=Driver)
  )+
  labs(
    x= "Average Start",
    y= "Average Finish",
    title= "Consistency is Key",
    subtitle= "Kyle Larson is one of the most consistent drivers in the field.",
    caption= "Source: Racing Reference | By: Beck Frazier"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 20, face = "bold")
  )

  geom_point(
  data=G7Totals, 
  aes(x=T5, y=T10, size=Led),
  color="grey",
  alpha = 0.3) +

    data=Champ10,
    aes(x=T5, y=T10, size=Led),
    color="red") +

    data=Champ10,
    aes(x=T5, y=T10, label=Driver)
  )+
  labs(

title: Are the Cleveland Browns Really Cursed at QB?
text:
Everybody knows that the laughing stock of football is the one and only Cleveland Browns. You could make the argument that it was Detroit and Cleveland, but Detroit has relieved themselves of that title with recent success. It is also known that Cleveland has gone through a metric ton of quarterbacks since coming back in 1999. But before anything, there’s one thing to go over: Passer Rating.
The most important thing to know is Quarterback Passer Rating. For reference, the highest a single game passer rating a quarterback can achieve is 158.3. There have been quarterbacks that have achieved this number, but no quarterback has ever finished with a career passer rating of 158.3. The record is currently held by Aaron Rodgers at 102.4. So this means that quarterbacks aren’t very good right? Well, sort of, yes. Only four quarterbacks have a career passer rating over 100.0 and all four of them are still active in the NFL. Meanwhile there are only 99 quarterbacks in the history of the NFL with a passer rating of at least 80.0.
Now that all of that has been taken care of, are Cleveland’s quarterbacks really that bad?


Code
library(tidyverse)
library(gt)
library(ggalt)
library(ggtext)
library(ggrepel)

TeamQB <- read_csv("Team1995to2024stats.csv")

TeamQB |>
  arrange(desc(AvgPassRating)) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(
    AvgWins = "Average Wins",
    AvgLosses = "Average Losses",
    TotalQB = "Total Quarterbacks",
    AvgPassRating = "Average Passer Rating",
    TotalINT = "Total Interceptions",
    TotalTD = "Total Touchdowns"
  ) |>
  tab_header(
  title = "Cleveland Quarterbacks Suck at Throwing a Football",
  subtitle = "Cleveland has the most starting QB's since 1999, but their average passer rating is astounding."
  ) |> tab_style(
    style = cell_text(color = "black", weight = "bold", align = "left"),
    locations = cells_title("title")
  ) |> tab_style(
    style = cell_text(color = "black", align = "left"),
    locations = cells_title("subtitle")
  ) |>
  tab_source_note(
    source_note = md("**By:** Beck Frazier | **Source:** Pro-Football Reference")
  ) |>
  tab_style(
    locations = cells_column_labels(columns = everything()),
    style = list(
      cell_borders(sides = "bottom", weight = px(3)),
      cell_text(weight = "bold", size=12)
    )
  ) |>
  opt_row_striping() |>
  opt_table_lines("none") |>
  tab_style(
    style = list(
      cell_fill(color = "orange"),
      cell_text(color = "black")

Carolina and Arizona have somehow had worse quarterbacks on average than Cleveland. Does it make sense? When you think about it at a glance, it doesn’t. However, when you think about it a little longer, it still doesn’t. Meanwhile, on the other end of the spectrum, Philadelphia, Green Bay, and New England are enjoying a meal at a Michelin five star restaurant. Their quarterbacks, on average, are, as the saying goes, the greatest thing since sliced bread.
Now, there is one big distinction between the teams I just mentioned. Since 1999, Green Bay, Philadelphia, and New England have all had franchise quarterbacks. In the case of Philadelphia, sometimes multiple franchise quarterbacks. For Arizona, Carolina, and Cleveland, these are teams that time and time again think they have franchise quarterbacks, but for one reason or another, can’t seem to hold onto a QB.


Code
ggplot() +
  geom_dumbbell(
    data=TeamQB,
    aes(y=reorder(Team, TotalTD), x=TotalTD, xend=TotalINT),
    size = 2,
    colour = "grey",
    colour_x = "green",
    colour_xend = "red") +
  labs(
    x= "Total Interceptions with Total Touchdowns",
    y= "",
    title="Do Your Team's Quarterbacks Throw Picks or Not?",
    subtitle = "If you aren't the Browns, Jets, or Bears, your team is probably fine. The Texans are three years behind.",
    caption= "Source: Pro-Football Reference | Beck Frazier"
  ) + 
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 18, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10),
    plot.title.position = "plot"
  )









Cleveland is bad. They are the only team that has thrown basically as many touchdowns as interceptions since 1999. There are some other close ones, but no one closer to a 1/1 touchdown to interception ratio than Cleveland. So what does that say? It says that Cleveland’s quarterbacks aren’t throwing for a lot of touchdowns while also throwing for more interceptions than any other team.
The three good teams that have been previously mentioned are towards the top in terms of touchdowns thrown. However, New England is the outlier with how few interceptions this team has thrown. Part of this is due to this guy named Tom Brady. He ended up being pretty good. No other team has thrown for under 200 interceptions since 1999. In fact, no team has thrown for under 300 interceptions.
Another point to make is that the Texans were not a franchise until 2002 so their data is a little behind the other teams.


Code
ClevelandQB <- TeamQB |> filter(Team == "Cleveland Browns")
GoodTeamQB <- TeamQB |> filter(Team == "Green Bay Packers" | Team == "New England Patriots" | Team == "Philadelphia Eagles")
BadTeamQB <- TeamQB |> filter(Team == "Arizona Cardinals" | Team == "Carolina Panthers")

ggplot() + 
  geom_point(
    data=TeamQB, 
    aes(x=AvgWins, y=AvgLosses, size=AvgPassRating),
    color="grey",
    alpha = 0.3
    ) +
  geom_point(
    data=ClevelandQB,
    aes(x=AvgWins, y=AvgLosses, size=AvgPassRating),
    color="orange",
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data=GoodTeamQB,
    aes(x=AvgWins, y=AvgLosses, size=AvgPassRating),
    color="green",
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data=BadTeamQB,
    aes(x=AvgWins, y=AvgLosses, size=AvgPassRating),
    color="red",
  ) +
  scale_size_continuous(
    name= "Average Passer Rating",
    range = c(2, 6),
    breaks = c(66, 70, 74, 78, 82, 86, 90)
  ) +
  geom_text_repel(
    data=ClevelandQB,
    aes(x=AvgWins, y=AvgLosses, label=Team)
  ) +
  geom_text_repel(
    data=GoodTeamQB,
    aes(x=AvgWins, y=AvgLosses, label=Team)
  )  +
  geom_text_repel(
    data=BadTeamQB,
    aes(x=AvgWins, y=AvgLosses, label=Team)
  ) +
  labs(
    x= "Average Wins",
    y= "Average Losses",
    title="Teams Struggle to Win With Bad Quarterbacks",
    subtitle = "Since 1999, Cleveland is the only team averaging less than 6 wins a season.",
    caption= "Source: Pro-Football Reference | Beck Frazier"
  ) + 
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 18, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10),
    plot.title.position = "plot"
  )









Oh boy. Cleveland fans should have looked away while they had the chance. The Browns are the only team in the league to average less than six wins a season since 1999. Cleveland is so bad, that they are averaging just over five wins every year. A stark contrast to the Browns team that moved to Baltimore. Even Carolina and Arizona are averaging about seven wins a season.
The three so called “good teams” are averaging 10 wins a season with New England averaging almost 11 wins every year. Do not play the fool into feeling bad for any of these teams when they aren’t very good for a couple of years.
To put it simply, Cleveland’s quarterbacks are bad. They’ve had bright spots with Baker Mayfield and Joe Flacco, but those were like hitting the lottery in terms of Cleveland’s performance. One would think though, that the Browns would’ve hit on a quarterback by now. Having 41 different starting quarterbacks is quite the impressive feat. Some say it should’ve been Baker, but the world may never know.

title: Is Kyle Larson the Best NASCAR Driver of the Gen 7 Era?
text:
There has been lots of talk about whether or not Kyle Larson is the best driver in the world. Well, that’s a difficult question to answer. To start, there’s countless different driving leagues and disciplines which makes it hard to determine if someone is the best driver in the world. It would be unfair to compare Larson to Marc Marquez (MotoGP) or to Max Verstappen (F1). Why? Well because the cars and motorcycles drive differently.
So how does one determine if Larson is as good as they say he is? By comparing him to his own competition. But this is difficult in its own right. NASCAR has a reputation of having drivers compete for championships or wins when they shouldn’t be. Take for example, Connor Zilisch. He won 10 races in the Xfinity Series this year but came 2nd in the championship. But this isn’t about the Xfinity Series, it’s about the Cup Series, and more specifically, the Generation 7 era of the Cup Series.
The Generation 7 era was introduced with the “Next Gen” car back in 2022. Since then NASCAR has seen three different champions, a plethora of winners, and a Kiwi who has taken the sport by storm. However, it’s not significant take a look at every driver who has competed in a race during the Gen 7 era. So instead, looking at drivers who compete full time and have raced more than half of the 144 races run in the last four seasons is a better cutoff. This will help decide if Larson is the best driver in the current era of NASCAR.


Code
library(tidyverse)
library(ggalt)
library(ggrepel)


G7Totals <- read_csv("DriversTotals.csv")


G7Larson <- G7Totals |>
  filter(
    Driver == "Larson"
  )
G7Logano <- G7Totals |>
  filter(
    Driver == "Logano"
  )
G7Chastain <- G7Totals |>
  filter(
    Driver == "Chastain"
  )
G7Bell <- G7Totals |>
  filter(
    Driver == "Bell"
  )
G7Hamlin <- G7Totals |>
  filter(
    Driver == "Hamlin"
  )
G7Elliott <- G7Totals |>
  filter(
    Driver == "Elliott"
  )
G7Briscoe <- G7Totals |>
  filter(
    Driver == "Briscoe"
  )
G7Blaney <- G7Totals |>
  filter(
    Driver == "Blaney"
  )
G7Byron <- G7Totals |>
  filter(
    Driver == "Byron"
  )
G7Reddick <- G7Totals |>
  filter(
    Driver == "Reddick"
  )
ggplot()+
  geom_bar(data=G7Totals, aes(x=reorder(Driver, Win), weight= Win), fill="lightgrey") +
  geom_bar(data=G7Larson, aes(x=reorder(Driver, Win), weight= Win), fill="blue") +
  geom_bar(data=G7Logano, aes(x=reorder(Driver, Win), weight= Win), fill="gold") +
  geom_bar(data=G7Chastain, aes(x=reorder(Driver, Win), weight= Win), fill="green") +
  geom_bar(data=G7Bell, aes(x=reorder(Driver, Win), weight= Win), fill="orange") +
  geom_bar(data=G7Hamlin, aes(x=reorder(Driver, Win), weight= Win), fill="purple") +
  geom_bar(data=G7Elliott, aes(x=reorder(Driver, Win), weight= Win), fill="lightblue") +
  geom_bar(data=G7Briscoe, aes(x=reorder(Driver, Win), weight= Win), fill="maroon") +
  geom_bar(data=G7Blaney, aes(x=reorder(Driver, Win), weight= Win), fill="yellow") +
  geom_bar(data=G7Byron, aes(x=reorder(Driver, Win), weight= Win), fill="red") +
  geom_bar(data=G7Reddick, aes(x=reorder(Driver, Win), weight= Win), fill="black") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    x= "Name of Driver",
    y= "Number of Wins in Gen 7 Era",
    title= "If You Ain't First, You're Last",
    subtitle= "Kyle Larson, in the Generation 7 era, is winning more than any other driver.",
    caption= "Source: Racing Reference | By: Beck Frazier"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 20, face = "bold")
  )









Kyle Larson is a winning machine. His 16 wins in this generation of NASCAR is the same amount of wins he had from 2014-2021. However, we see that there are other drivers who are not far behind the success that Larson has seen. Drivers like Denny Hamlin and William Byron have 14 wins in the last four years with Christopher Bell having 12.
Though, ten drivers have made the championship four in the current playoff format that NASCAR uses in the Gen 7 era. Larson is one of the ten drivers that have made the playoffs. So that should be reflected in other statistics. Wins doesn’t show how well you are throughout a race. Countless times the sport has seen someone fluke into a win but not perform well the rest of the year.
One of the biggest measures of this is where you finish in points. However, NASCAR’s point system is a little odd. Regardless of where you actually are in points, winning means you make it into the playoffs. This means you’re guaranteed to finish at least 16th in the points. But nonetheless, it’s your official points finish at the end of the year.
We can use this to our advantage though. If you’re winning consistently you should have a higher points finish than most drivers right?


Code

So does this mean that he now gets a say in being the best driver in the Gen 7 era? Depends on who you ask about that 2024 season. But that’s an argument for a different time.
Championships and wins may be nice and will be the things people remember, but consistency is how you get to the championships and wins. Where you finish and start matter. There’s more to racing than just winning. Which sounds really stupid, but it’s true. Ask Matt Crafton.

ggplot() + 
  geom_point(
  data=G7Totals, 
  aes(x=AvSt, y=AvFn, size=Win),
  color="grey",
  alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_point(
    data=Champ10,
    aes(x=AvSt, y=AvFn, size=Win),
    color="red") +
  geom_text_repel(
    data=Champ10,
    aes(x=AvSt, y=AvFn, label=Driver)
  )+
  labs(
    x= "Average Start",
    y= "Average Finish",
    title= "Consistency is Key",
    subtitle= "Kyle Larson is one of the most consistent drivers in the field.",
    caption= "Source: Racing Reference | By: Beck Frazier"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 20, face = "bold")
  )









Larson is in fact, not the best average finisher in the Gen 7 era. Chase Elliott and Christopher Bell are the only drivers who finish better than 13th on average. Plus, William Byron also finishes just barely better on average than Larson. Though, Larson is the only driver who starts, on average, better than 10th.
But this can be broken down even further. Average start and finish is nice and all, but it’s possible to see how many times a driver finishes in the top 5 and top 10. The stats can also help to see how many laps drivers are leading. Sometimes a driver will be leading for a majority of the race but then not end up with the win for various reasons. This helps determine who is running up at the front for these races.

ggplot() + 
  geom_point(
  data=G7Totals, 
  aes(x=T5, y=T10, size=Led),
  color="grey",
  alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_point(
    data=Champ10,
    aes(x=T5, y=T10, size=Led),
    color="red") +
  geom_text_repel(
    data=Champ10,
    aes(x=T5, y=T10, label=Driver)
  )+
  labs(
    x= "Top Fives",
    y= "Top Tens",
    title= "Consistency is Key Part 2",
    subtitle= "Kyle Larson is finishing in the Top 5 at an elite level.",
    caption= "Source: Racing Reference | By: Beck Frazier"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 20, face = "bold")
  )









Woah! Bell seems to be making a strong case here. He may not have the championships, but he has more top 10s than anyone and it’s not really close. He’s the only one with over 80 top 10s. However, Larson has more top 5s than anyone in the Gen 7 era.
So is Larson the best driver in the Gen 7 era? Well, the answer seems to be a resounding yes. Though it’s pretty close. Drivers like Bell, Byron and Hamlin all have cases that can be backed up. Only time will tell if these stats hold up until the next era of NASCAR.
